issues.legal_issue: An agreement of sale, power of attorney, and will used together as a substitute for a conveyance do not transfer title to immovable property.
material_facts: The judgment considered transactions in which a purported seller received the agreed price and delivered possession, but gave the purchaser an agreement of sale, a power of attorney, and a will instead of a registered deed of conveyance.
The documents were used as a purported mode of transferring property rather than as part of a genuine agency or development arrangement.
issues.conclusion: Such documents do not amount to a completed transfer or conveyance and do not transfer title; immovable property must be conveyed by a registered deed of conveyance.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 5 and 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a sale transfers ownership and a contract of sale does not itself create an interest in or charge on the property. Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908 require registration for instruments that create or transfer relevant rights in immovable property and provide that an unregistered instrument required to be registered does not affect the property. The Court relied on Narandas Karsondas v. S.A. Kamtam, Rambaran Prosad v. Ram Mohit Hazra, and Rambhau Namdeo Gajre v. Narayan Bapuji Dhotra. It rejected Asha M. Jain v. Canara Bank to the extent that it treated these arrangements as completed transfers.

predicates.power_of_attorney_used_as_transfer: The parties used a power of attorney as the purported transfer of the property instead of a conveyance.

issues.definition: When a sale of immovable property is purportedly completed through an agreement, power of attorney, or will without a registered conveyance, those documents do not transfer title.

issues.legal_issue: An agreement to sell immovable property does not itself transfer title or create an interest in the property, even if possession is delivered.
material_facts: The transaction form considered by the Court included an agreement confirming the sale terms, payment of the full price, and delivery of possession, with an undertaking to execute a sale deed later.
The purchaser might rely on the agreement as evidence of a completed transfer despite the absence of a registered conveyance.
issues.conclusion: An agreement to sell does not itself transfer title or create an interest or charge in the property, whether or not it is accompanied by possession, subject to the limited protection available under the law of part performance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 states that a contract for sale does not, of itself, create an interest in or charge on immovable property. Section 53A provides a limited protection concerning possession in part performance. The Court relied on Narandas Karsondas v. S.A. Kamtam and Rambaran Prosad v. Ram Mohit Hazra.

predicates.property_transfer_case: The dispute concerns whether documents used in a transaction involving immovable property transferred title.
predicates.contract_for_sale_of_immovable_property: The parties made a contract agreeing that immovable property would be sold on settled terms.
predicates.no_registered_conveyance: No registered deed of conveyance was executed for the sale.

issues.definition: A contract to sell immovable property without a registered conveyance does not itself create a property interest.

issues.legal_issue: Part performance may protect a transferee's possession against the transferor but does not give the transferee ownership or a right enforceable against a third party.
material_facts: The transaction form considered by the Court could involve a signed written contract, delivery or continuation of possession, acts in furtherance of the contract, and performance or willingness to perform by the transferee.
The Court explained that a transferee might rely on part performance to resist the transferor's attempt to disturb possession.
issues.conclusion: Part performance may provide a shield against the transferor, but it does not transfer ownership and cannot be used to assert that protection against a third party.
issues.legal_principle: Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 provides protection where the statutory conditions for part performance are met. The protection is limited to resisting the transferor or a person claiming under the transferor; it does not make the transferee the owner. The Court relied on Rambhau Namdeo Gajre v. Narayan Bapuji Dhotra.

predicates.transferee_performed_or_ready_to_perform: The transferee performed, or was willing to perform, the transferee's part of the contract.

issues.definition: Where the stated contract, possession, and performance predicates are met, part performance protects possession against the transferor but does not confer ownership.

issues.legal_issue: A power of attorney creates an agency and does not itself transfer title to immovable property, although an authorized attorney may execute a conveyance for the grantor.
material_facts: The transaction form considered by the Court included a power of attorney authorizing the purchaser or nominee to manage, deal with, or dispose of the property.
The Court distinguished those arrangements from an attorney executing a deed of conveyance under authority granted by the owner.
issues.conclusion: A power of attorney is not an instrument of transfer and does not give the attorney title; an attorney holder may nevertheless convey the grantor's title by executing a deed of conveyance within the authority granted.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 1A and 2 of the Powers of Attorney Act, 1882 concern the appointment and authority of an agent. A power of attorney operates as an agency under Chapter X of the Contract Act, 1872 and does not itself transfer title. The Court relied on State of Rajasthan v. Basant Nehata.

predicates.property_transfer_case: The dispute concerns whether documents used in a transaction involving immovable property transferred title.
predicates.power_of_attorney_granted: An owner authorized another person to act on the owner's behalf in relation to the property.
predicates.no_conveyance_executed_by_authorized_age: The authorized person did not execute a deed of conveyance for the owner.

issues.definition: When an owner grants authority to another person but no conveyance is executed under that authority, the power of attorney itself does not transfer title.

issues.legal_issue: A will is a revocable testamentary disposition effective after the testator's death and does not transfer immovable property during the testator's lifetime.
material_facts: The transaction form considered by the Court included a will in favour of the purchaser as a safeguard in case the purported seller died before a transfer was completed.
The Court noted that a will takes effect after death and may be revoked during the testator's lifetime.
issues.conclusion: A will is not a transfer inter vivos and does not itself convey title during the testator's lifetime; registration of the will does not alter that character.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 69 and 70 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 concern circumstances in which a will is revoked. A will is a testamentary disposition that takes effect on death and remains revocable during the testator's lifetime.

predicates.property_transfer_case: The dispute concerns whether documents used in a transaction involving immovable property transferred title.
predicates.will_made_by_property_owner: The property owner made a will purporting to bequeath the property to another person.
predicates.testator_is_alive: The person who made the will is alive.

issues.definition: A will made by a living property owner does not transfer the property before the owner's death.

issues.legal_issue: Genuine agency and development arrangements involving agreements and powers of attorney are not invalidated as purported property sales merely because they use those documents.
material_facts: The Court distinguished purported sales from an owner authorizing a relative or other person to manage the owner's affairs or execute a conveyance.
The Court also identified development arrangements in which a landowner authorizes a developer to execute agreements or conveyances to prospective purchasers.
issues.conclusion: The ruling against substitute agreement, power-of-attorney, and will transfers is not intended to affect the validity of genuine agency arrangements or development agreements and related powers of attorney.
issues.legal_principle: A power of attorney creates an agency that permits the agent to act for the principal within the authority granted; it is not itself a transfer of title. The Court distinguished this ordinary agency function and genuine development arrangements from purported completed sales made without conveyances.

issues.definition: A genuine arrangement authorizing management or conveyance is not invalidated when its documents are not used as a completed sale.

issues.legal_issue: The ruling does not require authorities to undo mutations already accepted and acted upon solely because of the ruling, and existing transaction documents retain limited uses.
material_facts: The Court considered the concern that persons had entered into such transactions before the judgment and might face hardship.

It stated that existing documents could continue to be treated as agreements of sale and could be used to seek specific performance, defend possession under part performance, or seek regularization in appropriate circumstances.
It also stated that mutations already accepted and acted upon by development, municipal, or revenue authorities need not be disturbed merely because of the ruling.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not make the ruling prospective; it reiterated the existing legal position while preserving the stated limited uses of existing documents and stating that previously acted-upon mutations need not be disturbed solely because of the ruling.
issues.legal_principle: The Court characterized its decision as a reiteration of the settled legal position. An existing agreement of sale may support a claim for specific performance or a defence of possession under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882; certain earlier documents may also be relied on to seek regularization. Administrative mutations already accepted and acted upon need not be undone merely on account of the decision.
